stem: You create the folder `app/blog/` and add `app/blog/layout.tsx` and `app/blog/PostCard.tsx`. Visiting `/blog` returns a 404. What is missing?

options.text: A `route.ts` file that exports a `GET` handler for the page
options.why: A Route Handler returns a raw HTTP response, not React UI, so it is not how you add a page.

options.text: A `page.tsx` file in `app/blog/`
options.why: A segment only becomes publicly routable once it has a `page` (or `route`) file.

options.text: `index.tsx`, the segment root
options.why: `index` is the Pages Router convention; the App Router uses `page`.

options.text: A `default.tsx` file so the segment has something to render
options.why: `default` is a fallback for parallel route slots, not the file that exposes a route.

explanation: Folders define URL segments, but a route is not publicly accessible until a `page.js` or `route.js` file exists in it. Layouts and colocated components such as `PostCard.tsx` are never routable on their own, which is why you can safely keep project files inside `app`.

stem: You want a `marketing` folder that groups pages and shares a layout without adding `/marketing` to any URL. Type the exact folder name to use.
explanation: Wrapping a folder name in parentheses, as in `(marketing)`, creates a route group. The folder is for organisation only and is omitted from the URL, so `app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx` serves `/about`.

stem: What does `params` resolve to for `app/shop/[...slug]/page.tsx` when you visit `/shop/a/b`?

options.text: `{ slug: 'a/b' }`
options.why: Catch-all params are an array of segments, not one joined string.

options.text: `{ slug: 'b' }`
options.why: A catch-all captures every remaining segment, not just the last one.
Each matched segment becomes one element of the array.
Extra segments are not spread into numbered keys.

explanation: A catch-all segment `[...slug]` matches `/shop/a`, `/shop/a/b`, `/shop/a/b/c` and so on, and passes the matched segments as an array: `/shop/a/b` gives `{ slug: ['a', 'b'] }`. Remember that `params` is a promise you must await.

stem: A helper file at `app/dashboard/utils/format.ts` (no underscore, no `page` or `route` file) can be requested in the browser at `/dashboard/utils/format`.

options.text: True
options.why: Only `page.js` and `route.js` make a segment routable; other colocated files are never served.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: colocated files without a `page` or `route` file are never routable.

explanation: Colocation is safe by default: even inside a routable segment, only the content returned by `page.js` or `route.js` is sent to the client. Private folders (`_utils`) are optional and mainly help organisation and avoid clashes with future conventions.

stem: Which line must an `error.tsx` file start with?

options.text: `'use client'`
options.why: Error boundaries are React class-style boundaries and must be Client Components.

options.text: `'use server'`
options.why: That marks Server Functions, not components that render UI.

options.text: `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`
options.why: This route segment config option does not make a file an error boundary.

options.text: `'use cache'`
options.why: Caching directives have nothing to do with error boundaries.

explanation: `error.js` wraps a segment in a React error boundary, and error boundaries must be Client Components, so the file needs the `'use client'` directive. A Server Component cannot act as an error boundary.

stem: Match each App Router file with what it does.

options.text: A Suspense fallback shown while the segment loads
An error boundary for unexpected runtime errors
UI shown when `notFound()` is thrown in the segment
A wrapper that remounts when its segment changes
A fallback for a parallel route slot after a full page load

explanation: `loading` is a Suspense boundary, `error` an error boundary, `not-found` renders for `notFound()`, `template` is like a layout but gets a key per segment so it remounts on navigation, and `default` renders for slots whose active state cannot be recovered after a hard navigation.

stem: What must the root layout (`app/layout.tsx`) render?

options.text: A `<head>` with a manual `<title>` and `<meta>` tags for SEO
options.why: The docs say not to add these by hand; use the Metadata API, which manages `<head>` for you.

options.text: The `<html>` and `<body>` tags around `children`
options.why: The root layout is the document shell, so it is required to define both tags.

options.text: A `<Suspense>` boundary so that `loading.tsx` files work
options.why: Next.js adds Suspense boundaries for `loading` files itself.

options.text: A `<Router>` provider
options.why: Routing is built in; there is no router provider to add.

explanation: The root layout is the top-most layout and must define `<html>` and `<body>`. Head tags such as `<title>` should come from the `metadata` export or `generateMetadata`, which handle streaming and de-duplication.

stem: What does `params` resolve to for `app/docs/[[...slug]]/page.tsx` when you visit exactly `/docs`?

options.text: Nothing: `/docs` returns a 404 because no segment matched
options.why: Double brackets make the catch-all optional, so the bare path matches.
An unmatched optional catch-all is `undefined`, not an empty array.
Catch-all params are arrays or undefined, never strings.

options.text: `{ slug: undefined }`
options.why: The route matches, but there are no segments to capture.

explanation: An optional catch-all `[[...slug]]` also matches the route without the parameter. For `/docs` the page renders with `{ slug: undefined }`, and for `/docs/a/b` with `{ slug: ['a', 'b'] }`. That is why its TypeScript type is `{ slug?: string[] }`.
reference: Next.js docs: Dynamic Route Segments (Optional Catch-all)

stem:
A page written for Next.js 14 still reads params synchronously after upgrading to Next.js 16: ```tsx export default function Page({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) { return

{params.slug}

} ``` What is the right fix?

options.text: Keep it: Next.js 16 still allows synchronous access with a warning
options.why: The temporary compatibility from Next.js 15 is fully removed in 16.

options.text: Add `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` so params arrive resolved
options.why: Rendering mode does not change the type of `params`; it is a promise either way.

options.text: Make the page `async`, type `params` as a `Promise`, and `await` it
options.why: In Next.js 16, `params` can only be read asynchronously, with `await` or React `use`.

options.text: Read the slug from `useParams()` inside this Server Component
options.why: `useParams` is a client hook and cannot run in a Server Component.

explanation: Next.js 15 made `params` and `searchParams` promises, with temporary synchronous compatibility. Next.js 16 removes synchronous access completely. Write `const { slug } = await params` in an async Server Component, or `use(params)` in a Client Component. The `next-async-request-api` codemod and the generated `PageProps<'/blog/[slug]'>` type help migrate.
reference: Next.js docs: Upgrading to version 16 (Async Request APIs)

stem: Which two of these files receive a `params` prop for `app/shop/[id]/`? (Choose two.)

options.text: `app/shop/[id]/layout.tsx`
options.why: Layouts receive `params` from the root down to that layout.

options.text: `app/shop/[id]/page.tsx`
options.why: Pages receive both `params` and `searchParams`.

options.text: `app/shop/[id]/loading.tsx`
options.why: Loading UI components do not accept any props.

options.text: `app/shop/[id]/not-found.tsx`
options.why: Not-found components do not accept any props.

options.text: `app/shop/[id]/error.tsx`
options.why: Error components receive `error` and `retry`/`reset`, not `params`.

explanation: `params` is passed to `layout`, `page`, `route`, `default` and `generateMetadata`. `loading.js` and `not-found.js` take no props, and `error.js` receives the error plus `retry` and `reset`. Inside those files, read params from a Client Component with `useParams()` if needed.

stem: A layout needs the current `?sort=` value to highlight a filter button. A developer adds `searchParams` to the layout's props, but it is always undefined. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Add `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` to the layout so it receives `searchParams`
options.why: Layouts never receive `searchParams`, whatever the rendering mode.

options.text: Pass it up from the page via context
options.why: Pages cannot pass data up to layouts, and context does not flow upwards.

options.text: Read it in a Client Component inside the layout with `useSearchParams()`
options.why: Client Components re-render on navigation, so they always see the current query.

options.text: Read `headers()` in the layout and parse the URL from the `referer` header
options.why: The referer is the previous page, and layouts would still not re-render on navigation.

explanation: Layouts do not re-render on navigation, so they are deliberately not given `searchParams`, which would go stale. Read the query in the page via its `searchParams` prop, or in a Client Component with `useSearchParams()`, which re-renders as the URL changes.

stem: An app has `app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx` and `app/(shop)/about/page.tsx`. What happens?

options.text: Both work: one at `/marketing/about` and one at `/shop/about`
options.why: Route group names are omitted from the URL, so both map to `/about`.

options.text: The first group alphabetically wins
options.why: There is no precedence rule between groups for the same path.

options.text: It is an error: both resolve to the same URL, `/about`
options.why: Routes in different groups must not resolve to the same URL path.

options.text: Next.js renders both pages one after the other at `/about`
options.why: Only parallel route slots render side by side, and groups are not slots.

explanation: Route groups organise files without changing URLs. Because `(marketing)` and `(shop)` are both dropped from the path, the two `about` pages conflict and Next.js reports an error. Give them different paths or merge them.

stem: An app has two root layouts: `app/(shop)/layout.tsx` and `app/(marketing)/layout.tsx`, with no `app/layout.tsx`. A user clicks a `<Link>` from `/cart` (shop) to `/blog` (marketing). What happens?

options.text: A normal client-side navigation that keeps all client state
options.why: Crossing root layouts can't reuse the document, so state is not kept.

options.text: A full page load, since the root layouts differ
options.why: Navigating across multiple root layouts always triggers a full page reload.

options.text: A 404, because `<Link>` cannot cross route groups
options.why: Links work across groups; only the navigation type changes.

options.text: Both root layouts render nested inside each other
options.why: Root layouts are separate documents with their own `<html>` and `<body>`.

explanation: Each root layout defines its own `<html>` and `<body>`, so moving between them needs a new document. Next.js therefore does a full page load instead of a client-side transition. This applies only when the root layouts differ; ordinary nested layouts navigate client-side.
reference: Next.js docs: Route Groups (Full page load)

stem: Put the special files of one route segment in their rendering order, from the outermost wrapper to the innermost.

options.text: `layout.tsx`
`template.tsx`
`error.tsx` (error boundary)
`loading.tsx` (Suspense boundary)
`not-found.tsx`
`page.tsx`

explanation: Within a segment the hierarchy is `layout` > `template` > `error` > `loading` > `not-found` > `page`. This order explains several behaviours: `error.tsx` cannot catch errors from the layout or template above it in the same segment, and `loading.tsx` cannot show a fallback for data the layout itself awaits.

stem: A developer adds `app/api-docs/route.ts` next to an existing `app/api-docs/page.tsx` so that the same URL can return JSON. What happens?

options.text: The route handler serves non-GET methods, and the page serves GET
options.why: Next.js does not split methods between a page and a handler at the same path.

options.text: The route handler takes over whenever the request asks for JSON
options.why: There is no content negotiation between `page` and `route` files.

options.text: A conflict: `route` and `page` can't share a segment
options.why: Both files would claim the same URL, which Next.js does not allow.

options.text: The page renders, and the route handler is quietly ignored
options.why: The clash is reported as an error, not silently resolved.

explanation: A segment can expose either UI (`page`) or an HTTP handler (`route`), not both. Put the JSON endpoint at a different path, such as `app/api-docs/data/route.ts` or `app/api/docs/route.ts`.

stem: `app/product/[id]/page.tsx` exports `generateStaticParams` returning ids `1` and `2`, plus `export const dynamicParams = false`. A request for `/product/3` is rendered on demand and cached.

options.text: True
options.why: With `dynamicParams = false`, ids not returned by `generateStaticParams` get a 404.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: with `dynamicParams = false`, ungenerated ids return 404.

explanation: `dynamicParams` defaults to `true`, meaning unknown params are rendered at request time. Setting it to `false` limits the route to the params you generated, and everything else returns 404. It replaces `fallback: false` from `getStaticPaths` in the Pages Router. Note that the option isn't available when Cache Components is enabled.

stem: A Client Component rendered by `app/dashboard/layout.tsx` calls `useSelectedLayoutSegment()`. What does it return when the user is at `/dashboard/analytics/monthly`?

options.text: `'analytics/monthly'`
options.why: Only catch-all segments are joined into one string; this route uses plain segments.

options.text: `'analytics'`
options.why: The hook returns the active segment one level below the calling layout.

options.text: `'monthly'`
options.why: That is two levels below; the hook only looks one level down.

options.text: `null`
options.why: `null` is returned only when there is no segment below, as at `/dashboard`.

explanation: `useSelectedLayoutSegment` reads the active segment one level below the layout it is called from, so `/dashboard/analytics/monthly` gives `'analytics'`, and `/dashboard` gives `null`. Use `useSelectedLayoutSegments()` for every active segment below. For a catch-all such as `[...slug]`, the matched segments come back joined, for example `'a/b/c'`.

stem: In a parallel route, Next.js cannot recover a slot's active page after a full page reload. Which special file name (without extension) does it render as the slot's fallback?
explanation: During soft navigation Next.js remembers each slot's active subpage. After a hard navigation it can't, so it renders the slot's `default.js`. In Next.js 16 every named slot needs an explicit `default.js` (a build fails without one); return `null` or call `notFound()` to choose the behaviour.

stem: An app removes `app/layout.tsx` and uses `app/(marketing)/layout.tsx` and `app/(shop)/layout.tsx` as two root layouts. Which statements are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: Each of the two layouts must render its own `<html>` and `<body>`
options.why: Any layout with no layout above it is a root layout, and every root layout defines the document.

options.text: The home page `/` must live inside one of the groups, for example `app/(marketing)/page.tsx`
options.why: Without a top-level layout, a page directly in `app/` would have no root layout.

options.text: Navigating from a marketing page to a shop page does a full page load
options.why: Crossing root layouts can't reuse the current document.

options.text: URLs gain a prefix, such as `/marketing/about`
options.why: Group names never appear in the URL.

options.text: Both layouts render on every page, one inside the other
options.why: Each page uses only the root layout of its own group.

explanation: Removing the top-level layout and adding a layout inside each route group creates multiple root layouts. Each must define `<html>` and `<body>`, the `/` route must be placed in one of the groups, and moving between groups triggers a full page load.
reference: Next.js docs: Route Groups and layout.js (Root Layout)

stem:
The tree is:

```text
app/
  layout.tsx
  error.tsx
  dashboard/
    layout.tsx   // throws during render
    error.tsx
    page.tsx
```

`app/dashboard/layout.tsx` throws while rendering `/dashboard`. Which error UI appears?

options.text: `app/dashboard/error.tsx`, the boundary closest to the failing file
options.why: An `error.js` does not wrap the layout of its own segment, so it can't catch this.

options.text: `app/error.tsx`, the boundary in the parent segment
options.why: The parent boundary wraps nested layouts, including `dashboard/layout.tsx`.

options.text: `app/global-error.tsx`, the only boundary that can handle a layout error
options.why: `global-error` handles errors in the root layout only.

options.text: None: layout errors aren't caught
options.why: Layout errors are caught by the nearest boundary above the layout.

explanation: In the hierarchy, `error.js` sits inside its segment's `layout.js`, so it catches errors from the page and from nested layouts below it, but not from the layout it sits next to. An error in `dashboard/layout.tsx` bubbles to `app/error.tsx`. Errors in the root layout need `app/global-error.tsx`.

stem: The only error boundary is `app/dashboard/error.tsx`. Visiting `/dashboard/settings`, the file `app/dashboard/settings/layout.tsx` throws during render. What happens?

options.text: `app/dashboard/error.tsx` renders in place of the settings subtree
options.why: An `error.js` wraps nested `layout.js` files in segments below it.

options.text: Nothing catches it, because only page errors reach `error.tsx`
options.why: Error boundaries catch rendering errors from nested layouts too.

options.text: Next.js needs `app/dashboard/settings/error.tsx`, so the default error page appears
options.why: The error bubbles to the nearest boundary above it.

options.text: The dashboard layout is unmounted and `global-error.tsx` renders
options.why: `global-error` is only for errors in the root layout or template.

explanation: `error.js` wraps `loading.js`, `not-found.js`, `page.js` and nested `layout.js` files. The settings layout is nested below the dashboard segment, so `dashboard/error.tsx` catches the error. The dashboard layout itself stays mounted and interactive around the error UI.

stem: Without Cache Components, `app/account/layout.tsx` awaits `cookies()` and makes a slow uncached fetch, and `app/account/loading.tsx` exists. When users navigate to `/account`, they see the old page frozen until everything loads, and the loading UI never appears. Why?

options.text: `loading.tsx` only works when the page is a Client Component
options.why: Loading files are Suspense boundaries and work with Server Component pages.

options.text: The fallback is never prefetched, so `loading.tsx` is skipped
options.why: Loading UI is prefetched; the issue is where the slow work happens.

options.text: `loading.tsx` is nested inside the layout, below its data
options.why: The layout must finish before its children, including the fallback, can render.

options.text: `cookies()` turns off streaming for the whole app
options.why: Request-time APIs make the route dynamic but do not disable streaming.

explanation: `loading.js` wraps the page and nested layouts in Suspense, but not the layout of its own segment. Without Cache Components, navigation blocks until the layout finishes rendering. Fix it by moving the slow work into `page.tsx` or by wrapping that part of the layout in its own `<Suspense>`.
reference: Next.js docs: loading.js and layout.js (Interaction with loading.js)

stem:
The tree is:

```text
app/
  layout.tsx
  template.tsx
  blog/
    template.tsx
    [slug]/page.tsx
```

A user navigates client-side from `/blog/first-post` to `/blog/second-post`. Which templates remount?

options.text: Both templates, because the URL changed
options.why: Templates remount only when the segment at their own level changes.

options.text: Only `app/template.tsx`
options.why: The first segment is still `blog`, so the root template's key stays the same.

options.text: Only `app/blog/template.tsx`
options.why: The segment below `blog` changed, so only the blog-level template gets a new key.

options.text: Neither, because templates only remount on a full page load
options.why: Remounting on client navigation is exactly what templates are for.

explanation: Each template gets a key for its own segment level. Going from `/blog/first-post` to `/blog/second-post` keeps the first segment (`blog`), so the root template stays mounted, while the blog template's child segment changes and it remounts. Client state and effects inside it reset.

stem: A `template.tsx` remounts its children when only the query string changes, for example from `/products?page=1` to `/products?page=2`.

options.text: True
options.why: Templates remount when their segment or its dynamic params change; search params don't trigger a remount.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: a query-string change keeps the template's key, so it does not remount.

explanation: Templates are keyed by route segments, including dynamic params, so `/blog/a` to `/blog/b` remounts a template at that level. Changing only `searchParams` keeps the same key, so client state inside the template survives. Use a `key` derived from the query yourself if you need a reset.

stem: A dashboard layout renders two slots. `@team` has `page.tsx` and `settings/page.tsx`, while `@analytics` has only `page.tsx` and `default.tsx`. The user starts at `/`, clicks a `<Link>` to `/settings`, then refreshes the browser. What does `@analytics` show after the click and after the refresh?

options.text: Its previous page after the click; `default.tsx` after the refresh
options.why: Soft navigation keeps the active state of unmatched slots, and a reload falls back to `default`.

options.text: It shows `default.tsx` after the click and after the refresh
options.why: On soft navigation Next.js keeps the slot's previous page instead.

options.text: A 404 after the click, then its `page.tsx` after the refresh
options.why: Unmatched slots aren't a 404 on soft navigation, and a reload can't recover `page.tsx`.

options.text: Its `page.tsx` both times, because a slot always shows its own root page
options.why: After a hard navigation, Next.js can't know which page was active and renders `default`.

explanation: Next.js tracks each slot's active subpage during soft navigation and keeps it even when the slot has no match for the new URL. After a full page load that state is lost, so slots without a match render their `default.js`. This is why every named slot needs a `default.js` in Next.js 16.

stem: A team upgrades an app with parallel route slots to Next.js 16. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Every named slot such as `@modal` needs an explicit `default.js`, or the build fails
options.why: Next.js 16 made `default.js` mandatory for parallel route slots.

options.text: A `default.js` that calls `notFound()` keeps the old 404-on-reload behaviour
options.why: The upgrade guide gives this exact pattern for keeping the previous behaviour.

options.text: Slots now add a URL segment, so `@modal/login` is served at `/@modal/login`
options.why: Slots are not route segments and never change the URL.

options.text: `default.js` renders on every soft navigation, replacing the slot's page
options.why: It is only used when the active state can't be recovered, such as after a reload.

options.text: `default.js` cannot read `params`, because it is only a fallback
options.why: `default.js` receives `params` as a promise, like a page.

explanation: Next.js 16 requires an explicit `default.js` for every parallel route slot. Return `null` to render nothing, or call `notFound()` to keep the old 404 behaviour. `default.js` is only used when Next.js can't recover a slot's state, and it receives `params` from the root down to the slot.
reference: Next.js docs: Upgrading to version 16 (Parallel Routes default.js)

stem: A gallery at `app/page.tsx` links to photos at `app/photo/[id]/page.tsx`. To open photos as a modal, the root layout renders a `@modal` slot. Which file intercepts `/photo/[id]` inside that slot?

options.text: `app/@modal/(..)photo/[id]/page.tsx`
options.why: `(..)` would look one segment up, but slots don't count as segments, so this goes above the root.

options.text: `app/@modal/(.)photo/[id]/page.tsx`
options.why: `@modal` is not a segment, so `photo` is on the same level and `(.)` matches it.

options.text: `app/photo/@modal/[id]/page.tsx`
options.why: This defines a slot under `photo`; nothing here intercepts a route.

options.text: `app/@modal/photo/[id]/page.tsx`
options.why: Without a `(.)` style prefix this is a regular slot page, not an interception.

explanation: Intercepting conventions are relative to route segments, not folders, and `@slot` folders are not segments. From `app/@modal`, the `photo` segment is at the same level, so the folder is `(.)photo`. Clicking a link shows the modal; a direct visit or refresh renders the real photo page.

stem: A photo modal is built with `app/@modal/(.)photo/[id]/page.tsx`. A user opens it by clicking a thumbnail, then refreshes the browser on `/photo/42`. What renders?

options.text: The same modal, layered over the gallery
options.why: Interception only happens on client-side navigation, not on a full page load.

options.text: The full photo page, with no interception
options.why: On a reload or direct visit, the real route renders instead of the intercepting one.

options.text: A 404, because `/photo/42` only exists as a modal
options.why: The real photo route still exists and serves the URL directly.

options.text: The gallery with the modal closed, ignoring the photo id
options.why: The URL points at the photo, so the photo page renders.

explanation: Intercepting routes mask the URL during client navigation, showing `/photo/42` in a modal over the gallery. Shareable links and refreshes load the route normally, so the user sees the full photo page. The `@modal` slot renders its `default.js`, typically `null`.

stem: A login modal lives in `app/@auth/(.)login/page.tsx`, and `app/@auth/default.tsx` returns `null`. Clicking a `<Link href="/about">` inside the modal navigates to `/about`, but the modal stays on screen. What fixes this?

options.text: Call `router.refresh()` after every navigation to re-render the slot
options.why: Refreshing re-renders the same active slot state; the slot still has no match.

options.text: Add `'use client'` to `default.tsx` so it renders on navigation
options.why: `default.tsx` is not used on soft navigation, whether or not it is a Client Component.

options.text: Add `app/@auth/[...catchAll]/page.tsx` that returns `null`
options.why: On soft navigation, an unmatched slot keeps its old page; matching it to `null` closes the modal.

options.text: Move the modal into `app/login/page.tsx` so it is no longer a slot
options.why: That removes the modal behaviour instead of closing it correctly.

explanation: On client-side navigation, a slot that doesn't match the new URL keeps rendering its previous page, which here is the modal. Give the slot a match that renders nothing: `app/@auth/page.tsx` for `/` and a catch-all `app/@auth/[...catchAll]/page.tsx` for other routes. Alternatively, close the modal with `router.back()`.
reference: Next.js docs: Parallel Routes (Closing the modal)

options.text: None: the admin slot is skipped entirely for non-admins
options.why: Both slots render on the server whichever one the layout returns.

options.text: Both slots render, so the admin data is fetched for every user
options.why: The conditional only picks what is shown; `@admin` still runs its fetches.

options.text: Only that `checkUserRole()` can be cached across users
options.why: Caching is not the issue; the slot executes for everyone.

options.text: Parallel routes cannot read cookies, so the role check always fails
options.why: Slots and layouts can read request data like any Server Component.

explanation: With parallel routes, both slots render on the server whatever the layout returns. The admin page's data fetches run for every user, and its output is included in the response sent to the browser. Authorize inside each slot's page or in a Data Access Layer, not only in the layout that picks the slot.

stem: For `app/products/[category]/[product]`, which two statements about `generateStaticParams` are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: `app/products/[category]/layout.tsx` can generate params for `[category]` only
options.why: You can generate params for segments at or above a file, never below it.

options.text: A child `generateStaticParams` runs once for each params object the parent returns
options.why: The child receives the parent's params and generates its own segments from them.

options.text: It runs again for each path on every ISR revalidation
options.why: `generateStaticParams` is not called again during revalidation.

options.text: Returning nothing (`undefined`) is treated the same as an empty array
options.why: You must return an array; otherwise the route is rendered dynamically.

options.text: With Cache Components, returning `[]` is the usual way to defer every path
options.why: With Cache Components, an empty array is a build error; return at least one param.

explanation: Params can be generated top down (parent first, then the child once per parent result) or bottom up (the page generates both). A layout cannot generate params for segments below it. `generateStaticParams` must return an array, isn't re-run during ISR, and under Cache Components must return at least one param.

stem: Match each route file and URL with the `params` object it resolves to.

options.text: `{ slug: undefined }`
`{ category: '1', item: '2' }`

explanation: A single dynamic segment gives a string, a catch-all gives an array of the matched segments, an optional catch-all at its bare path gives `undefined`, and two nested dynamic segments give one key each. In every case `params` is a promise you await.

options.text: `notFound()` only works when the caller writes `return notFound()`
options.why: Calling it is enough; it throws and stops execution either way.

options.text: `notFound()` throws, and this `try/catch` swallows it
options.why: The not-found UI never renders. Rethrow it, for example with `unstable_rethrow`.

options.text: `notFound()` can only be called from inside a page component
options.why: It also works in Server Components, Server Functions and Route Handlers.

options.text: The segment has no `not-found.tsx`, so `notFound()` does nothing
options.why: Without one, the nearest parent or the default 404 renders instead.

explanation: `notFound()` works by throwing a special error that travels up to the nearest not-found boundary. A broad `try/catch` intercepts it, so nothing renders the 404 UI. Call `unstable_rethrow(err)` at the top of the catch block, or keep the `notFound()` call outside the `try`.

stem: A blog page shows its shell immediately and loads the article inside `<Suspense>`. When the post is missing, the article component calls `notFound()`. Analytics shows these URLs returning HTTP 200, not 404. What is happening, and how do you get a real 404?

options.text: A bug: `notFound()` always sets 404, so a proxy must be rewriting the status
options.why: Once streaming starts, the status code can no longer change.

options.text: The not-found UI failed to render; add `not-found.tsx` to restore the 404
options.why: Adding the file changes the UI, not the status of a response that is already streaming.

options.text: Streaming had started, so 200 plus `noindex`; check before streaming
options.why: The headers were already sent. For a true 404, check the slug before the stream, for example in `proxy`.

options.text: Suspense boundaries always use status 200; replace them with `loading.tsx`
options.why: `loading.tsx` is also a Suspense boundary and streams with 200 too.

explanation: When a page streams, the 200 status and headers are sent with the shell. A `notFound()` thrown later inside Suspense renders the not-found UI in place and adds `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">`, giving a soft 404 that search engines won't index. For a real 404, make the existence check before anything suspends, or in `proxy`.
reference: Next.js docs: loading.js (Status Codes) and notFound

stem: A team wants authenticated users without the admin role to see a custom 403 page by calling `forbidden()`. Which statements are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: It requires enabling the experimental `authInterrupts` option in `next.config`
options.why: `forbidden` and `unauthorized` are experimental and behind this flag.

options.text: It cannot be called in the root layout
options.why: The docs list the root layout as unsupported for `forbidden()`.

options.text: A `forbidden()` left in an un-awaited promise renders no 403 UI
options.why: The throw happens where nothing catches it, so no boundary handles it.

options.text: Calling it inside `<Suspense>` after streaming still gives a 403 status
options.why: Once streaming has begun, the response status stays 200.

options.text: You must write `return forbidden()` or execution continues
options.why: It throws, with a `never` return type, so code after it never runs.

explanation: `forbidden()` throws an interrupt that renders `forbidden.tsx` with a 403 status, but only with `experimental.authInterrupts` enabled. It can't be used in the root layout, must be awaited where it may throw, and inside a streaming Suspense boundary the status stays 200. For a real 403 in that case, check in `proxy`.

stem: Which statements about `error.tsx` in Next.js 16 are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: In production, errors from Server Components reach it with a generic message and a `digest`
options.why: This prevents leaking server details; the digest matches server logs.

options.text: `retry()` re-fetches and re-renders the boundary's children
options.why: `retry` became stable in 16.3 and is the recommended recovery.

options.text: It doesn't catch errors thrown inside a `click` event handler
options.why: Error boundaries catch rendering errors, not errors in event handlers.

options.text: `reset()` is preferred over `retry()` for recovering from a failed fetch
options.why: The docs recommend `retry()`; `reset()` clears state without re-fetching.

options.text: It can be a Server Component if it doesn't use hooks
options.why: Error boundaries must always be Client Components.

explanation: `error.js` receives `error` (a generic message plus `digest` for Server Component errors in production), `retry()` to re-fetch and re-render, and `reset()` to clear the error without re-fetching. Like every React error boundary it catches errors during rendering, not in event handlers or async callbacks.

stem: An error in the root layout shows `app/global-error.tsx`, but it appears unstyled and ignores the dark theme. Which two statements explain this or are required? (Choose two.)

options.text: It replaces the root layout, so it must render its own `<html>` and `<body>`
options.why: When active it replaces the root layout entirely, document shell included.

options.text: It doesn't get your global styles or theme class; import or apply them in the file
options.why: It renders its own document, so the app's theme never reaches it.

options.text: It inherits the root layout's fonts and CSS, so the theme bug is elsewhere
options.why: Because it replaces the root layout, nothing from that layout applies.

options.text: It should export `metadata` to set the page title and theme color
options.why: It is a Client Component, so `metadata` exports aren't supported; use `<title>`.

options.text: It only renders in production, so dark mode cannot be tested in development
options.why: Since 15.2, `global-error` is shown in development too.

explanation: `global-error.js` handles errors in the root layout or template by replacing them, so it must define `<html>` and `<body>` and bring its own styles, fonts and theme. As a Client Component it can't export `metadata`; use React's `<title>` instead.

stem: With `cacheComponents` enabled, `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` has `generateStaticParams` returning `[]` so that every post renders on first request. What happens at build time?

options.text: Every post is built on first request and then cached
options.why: That is the behaviour without Cache Components, not with it.

options.text: Build error: it must return at least one param
options.why: Next.js needs a sample param to validate the route's use of request-time APIs.

options.text: The route silently becomes fully dynamic
options.why: An empty array is reported as an error, not quietly accepted.

options.text: Next.js reads all slugs from `generateMetadata` instead
options.why: `generateMetadata` does not supply params for prerendering.

explanation: With Cache Components, the build runs the route with sample params to check that `cookies()`, `headers()` and `searchParams` are used correctly. An empty array is a build error. Return at least one real param. If you truly have none at build time, use a placeholder that you handle with `notFound()`, at the cost of weaker build-time validation.

stem: A team enables `cacheComponents` in Next.js 16 and keeps `export const dynamicParams = false` on a product page to 404 unknown ids. What should they expect?

options.text: It works as before: ids not returned by `generateStaticParams` give a 404
options.why: The option is removed under Cache Components, so it no longer has this effect.

options.text: It makes every unknown id render on demand, the opposite of before
options.why: It isn't inverted; it is unavailable.

options.text: `dynamicParams` is unavailable here; call `notFound()` yourself
options.why: Validate the id in the page and call `notFound()` for unknown values.

options.text: It turns the whole route into a static export
options.why: No segment option does that; `output: 'export'` is a project-wide setting.

explanation: In Next.js 16, the `dynamic`, `dynamicParams`, `revalidate` and `fetchCache` segment options are removed when Cache Components is enabled. To reject unknown params, look the record up and call `notFound()` when it doesn't exist, or block invalid ids earlier in `proxy`.
reference: Next.js docs: Route Segment Config and dynamicParams

stem: A feed page is `app/feed/page.tsx`, and photos live at `app/photo/[id]/page.tsx`. The feed layout renders a `@modal` slot at `app/feed/@modal/`. Which folder makes a click from `/feed` to `/photo/7` open in that slot?

options.text: `app/feed/@modal/(..)(..)photo/[id]/page.tsx`
options.why: This counts `@modal` as a level, but slots aren't segments.

options.text: `app/feed/@modal/(..)photo/[id]/page.tsx`
options.why: Ignoring the slot, the current segment is `feed`, so `photo` is one level up.

options.text: `app/feed/@modal/(.)photo/[id]/page.tsx`
options.why: `(.)` would match `/feed/photo/7`, a sibling inside `feed`.

options.text: `app/feed/@modal/(...)feed/photo/[id]/page.tsx`
options.why: From the root this would target `/feed/photo/[id]`, which doesn't exist.

explanation: Count route segments, not folders. `@modal` is a slot, so code in `app/feed/@modal` is at the `feed` segment level. `/photo/[id]` hangs off the root, one segment above `feed`, so the folder is `(..)photo`. This is the same reasoning as the docs' gallery example, where the path is two folders up but only one segment.

stem: With Cache Components enabled, `app/shop/[category]/layout.tsx` (no `generateStaticParams`) starts with `const { category } = await params` and then renders a large static navigation. The build reports that this layout can't be part of the static shell. What is the recommended fix?

options.text: Add `export const dynamic = 'force-static'` to the layout
options.why: Segment options like `dynamic` are removed under Cache Components.

options.text: Await `params` in a child component inside `<Suspense>`
options.why: The layout stays prerenderable, and only the part that needs the param waits.

options.text: Read the category with `useParams()` in the layout itself
options.why: The layout is a Server Component, and client hooks can't be used there.

options.text: Move the layout into a route group so it no longer receives params
options.why: Groups don't change which params a layout receives.

explanation: Without `generateStaticParams`, params are request-time data under Cache Components. Awaiting them at the top of a layout pulls the whole layout out of the static shell. Pass the promise down to the component that needs it, inside a `<Suspense>` boundary, so the navigation prerenders and only that child streams in.
reference: Next.js docs: Dynamic Route Segments (With Cache Components)

stem:
A request for `/dashboard/settings` uses these files. Put them in render-nesting order, from outermost to innermost.

```text
app/layout.tsx
app/error.tsx
app/dashboard/layout.tsx
app/dashboard/loading.tsx
app/dashboard/settings/page.tsx
```

options.text: `app/layout.tsx`
`app/error.tsx`
`app/dashboard/layout.tsx`
`app/dashboard/loading.tsx`
`app/dashboard/settings/page.tsx`

explanation: Each segment renders layout > template > error > loading > not-found > children, and a child segment's files nest inside its parent's. So `app/error.tsx` wraps the dashboard layout, which is why it catches that layout's errors. The dashboard loading boundary sits inside the dashboard layout and covers the settings page.

stem: A project has both `app/` at the root and `src/app/`. Next.js ignores `src/app/` and routes from the root `app/` directory.

options.text: True
options.why: When `app` (or `pages`) exists in the project root, the `src/app` (or `src/pages`) folder is ignored.

options.text: False
options.why: It is neither an error nor a merge: the root `app` folder wins and `src/app` is ignored.

explanation: The `src` folder is an optional place for the `app` or `pages` directory. If both exist, the root-level directory wins and `src/app` is ignored, a common cause of "my routes don't exist" bugs after a partial move. `public`, config files and `.env` files stay in the project root either way.

stem: A breadcrumb Client Component in `app/layout.tsx` calls `useSelectedLayoutSegments()`. At `/cart`, served by `app/(shop)/cart/page.tsx`, it shows "(shop) / cart". What explains this, and what is the fix?

options.text: A bug: route groups never appear in hook results, so the cache is stale
options.why: The docs say the returned segments do include route groups.

options.text: Use `usePathname()` and split it, because segment hooks are deprecated
options.why: The segment hooks are not deprecated.

options.text: The hook includes route groups; filter out `(`-prefixed items
options.why: Groups are real segments in the tree, though not in the URL.

options.text: Rename the folder to `_shop` so it is hidden from both URLs and hooks
options.why: An underscore makes a private folder, which opts the whole folder out of routing.

explanation: `useSelectedLayoutSegments` returns the active segments below the calling layout, and that list includes route group segments such as `(shop)`, even though groups don't appear in the URL. The docs suggest filtering out items that start with a parenthesis before rendering breadcrumbs.

stem: Folders that start with `_` are private and excluded from routing. You need a public URL segment `/_preview`. Type the folder name that produces it.
explanation: Prefixing a folder with an underscore opts it and all its subfolders out of routing. To create a URL segment that really starts with an underscore, use the URL-encoded underscore: `%5Fpreview` serves `/_preview`.
